summary: Codex is a **133-crate Rust workspace** shaped as a layered hub: a serde-typed `codex-protocol` vocabulary at the bottom (68 dependents), a `codex-core` engine that owns the session loop and pulls in 61 workspace crates, and thin frontends (`tui`, `exec`, `cli`) that reach the engine through an app-server JSON-RPC layer. Commands the model wants to run cross a **process and OS-sandbox boundary**: `codex-sandboxing` selects Seatbelt, seccomp plus Landlock or bubblewrap, or a Windows restricted token, while `exec-server` can move execution to another machine over the same protocol. The production dependency graph has **no cycles**; the notable structural defects are the god-crate `core` that the repo's own AGENTS.md warns against, a `protocol` crate that depends on the policy engine and network-proxy service crates it is supposed to sit beneath, and a TUI that mostly uses the app-server client but still imports the executor directly. Security boundaries are well structured but the **Windows sandbox defaults to disabled** and the manager silently degrades to `SandboxType::None` there; MCP servers and hooks run outside the command sandbox by design.

findings.title: Layered crate hub around a session-loop engine, with execution pushed across a process boundary
findings.description: The `codex-rs` Cargo workspace declares 133 member crates and the manifest graph reads as **four layers**. At the bottom sits `codex-protocol` (68 in-workspace dependents) plus small `utils/*` crates. Above it are service crates: `config`, `sandboxing`, `network-proxy`, `execpolicy`, `exec-server`, `rollout`/`state`, model clients. `codex-core` is the engine hub: it depends on 61 workspace crates and is depended on by 23, and it runs every conversation as an **async actor**: a bounded submission channel in, an unbounded event channel out. The top layer is frontends and API: `app-server` exposes the engine over JSON-RPC on stdio, Unix socket or WebSocket, and `tui` consumes it through `app-server-client` rather than linking `core`. Anything the model executes is transformed by `codex-sandboxing` into an OS-sandboxed child process, or shipped to a remote `exec-server`, so the **execution boundary is a process boundary** by construction. The structure optimises for many entry points sharing one engine and for moving execution off the host, at the price of a very large `core`.

TUI links the API client, not codex-core

findings.title: codex-core: the conversation engine that owns sessions, turns, tool dispatch and policy decisions
findings.description: `codex-core` is responsible for running a thread: it holds the `Session` and `CodexThread` types, the `submission_loop` that consumes user submissions, the tool-call pipeline including `exec` and `apply_patch`, and the in-engine glue for config, exec policy, hooks, MCP and guardian review. It re-exports network-policy types from `codex-network-proxy` and turn-input types from `codex-protocol`, which is why frontends rarely need the lower crates. It depends on **61 workspace crates** and 23 depend on it, including `app-server`, `exec`, `cli`, `mcp-server` and every `ext/*` extension except `ext/skills` and `ext/extension-api`. Replacing it means replacing the product; it is the one component with no substitute.

evidence.note: core re-exports lower-layer policy types as its own API
exec-policy evaluation lives inside the engine

findings.title: Execution cluster: sandboxing, platform sandboxes, exec-server, arg0 dispatch and process hardening
findings.description: Nine crates together own **how a model-requested command becomes a confined child process**. `codex-sandboxing` is the platform-neutral manager: it picks a `SandboxType` and rewrites an argv into a Seatbelt, Linux or Windows wrapper invocation. `linux-sandbox` (bubblewrap launcher, seccomp, Landlock), `windows-sandbox-rs` (restricted token) and `bwrap` (a bundled bubblewrap build) are the platform backends. `execpolicy` is a rule engine deciding allow/prompt/forbid per command prefix, used by `core` and `config`. `exec-server` plus `exec-server-protocol` turn process spawning into a JSON-RPC service that can run locally or on a remote environment. `arg0` multiplexes the single `codex` binary into these helpers by executable name or first argument, and `process-hardening` runs pre-main to disable core dumps and ptrace. `network-proxy` belongs here functionally but sits below `protocol` in the graph (see the violations group).

findings.title: Frontends and the app-server API layer
findings.description: `app-server` is the **product API**: it hosts `codex-core`, wires in every `ext/*` extension, and speaks `app-server-protocol` JSON-RPC over the transports in `app-server-transport` (stdio, Unix socket, WebSocket, and a remote-control mode with its own kill switch). `app-server-client` is the in-tree consumer library. `tui` is a client of that API and does not link `core`; `exec` (headless) links both the client and `core`; `cli` is the binary shell that mounts every subcommand, including `mcp-server`, `exec-server`, `responses-api-proxy` and `cloud-tasks`. The 54-dependency `app-server` and 44-dependency `cli` are hubs by role, not by accident: they are the composition roots.

remote-control transport has its own disable switch

findings.title: Two extension clusters: in-tree ext/* contributors and external MCP, plugin, skill and hook surfaces
findings.description: Two different things are called extensions. The **in-tree** `ext/*` crates (agent, goal, guardian-v2, image-generation, mcp, memories, queue, skills, web-search, git-attribution, connectors) implement contributor traits from `ext/extension-api` and are registered by `app-server`; ten of them still depend on `core` directly, so they are engine plugins compiled into the binary, not a stable public extension point. The **external** surfaces are the crates for third-party code: `rmcp-client` launches MCP servers as stdio child processes or connects over HTTP, `mcp-server` exposes Codex itself as an MCP server (its own header still calls it a prototype), `codex-mcp` holds the MCP bindings and capability negotiation, `plugin` and `utils/plugins` model marketplace plugin packages, `skills` loads skill folders, and `hooks` runs user-configured hook commands with a trust gate.

findings.title: Sokrates primary decomposition: right at the top, misleading at two seams
findings.description: The 17-component `primary` decomposition matches the crate layering well for `core engine`, `app-server API`, `TUI frontend`, `persistence` and `configuration`. Three placements mislead. **`network-proxy` is filed under `sandboxing & policy`** but in the manifest graph it is a dependency of `protocol`, i.e. it sits in the bottom layer under everything; the component view therefore shows the vocabulary layer depending on the sandbox layer. **`apply-patch` is filed under `core engine`** while it depends on `exec-server`, making the engine component appear to depend on the executor at a point where the real edge is a helper-dispatch one. **`shared infrastructure` is a remainder bucket** defined as `.*/codex-rs/.*` minus every other component, so it collects `otel`, `git-utils`, `utils/*` and unassigned crates without a shared responsibility. The `by-layer` decomposition is closer to the truth for direction questions.

evidence.note: network-proxy is below protocol, not beside the sandbox

findings.recommendation: Move `network-proxy` (and `execpolicy`) into a `policy vocabulary` component next to `protocol`, move `apply-patch` into the exec-server component, and split `shared infrastructure` into `observability (otel)` and `utils`. Then the component dependency view will show the same direction as the manifests.

findings.title: codex-protocol is the shared vocabulary that 68 crates agree on
findings.description: `codex-protocol` defines the **serde-typed contract** for everything that crosses a seam inside Codex: `SandboxPolicy`, `AskForApproval`, `PermissionProfile`, thread and turn items, MCP policy, the `Event`/`Submission` pair. 68 of 133 crates depend on it and it has no dependency on `core`, so it holds as the one-directional floor of the workspace. Its versioning is by serde attributes rather than by version numbers: renames and aliases such as `on-failure` for `OnRequest` are the compatibility mechanism, and a `legacy_events` module keeps older wire shapes decodable. That makes the contract wide but shallow: any field added here reaches every layer at once.

findings.title: app-server-protocol: the versioned JSON-RPC contract between engine and clients
findings.description: `app-server-protocol` is the **external API contract**: request, response and notification types with schema export for TypeScript and other SDKs, organised into `v1` and `v2` modules that are both exported. Thirteen crates depend on it, on both sides of the process boundary (`app-server`, `app-server-client`, `tui`, `exec`, `cli`, `core`). The contract is what lets `tui` be a pure client. It is also the reason `core` depends on `app-server-protocol` rather than the reverse: the engine produces API-shaped items directly, which couples the engine to the API version.

findings.title: exec-server-protocol: the engine-to-executor contract that makes execution location-independent
findings.description: `exec-server-protocol` defines the JSON-RPC envelope the engine uses to spawn and control processes through `exec-server`: `InitializeParams`, `ExecParams`, environment capabilities, and a **network-policy round trip** in which the executor asks the engine whether a connection should be allowed and receives an `ExecServerNetworkPolicyDecision`. Because the same contract runs over a local WebSocket or a Noise-encrypted relay to a remote environment, the sandbox can be on another machine without the engine changing. 17 crates depend on `exec-server`, including `apply-patch`, `arg0` and the `ext/*` crates that need to run commands, which makes the executor the second hub after `core`.

findings.title: ext/extension-api: trait-based contributor seam for in-tree extensions
findings.description: `ext/extension-api` defines a family of **contributor traits** (`ToolContributor`, `McpServerContributor`, `ContextContributor`, `TurnLifecycleContributor`, `ApprovalReviewContributor` and others) plus an `ExtensionRegistryBuilder` that `app-server` fills. The seam is intended to let features be added without touching `core`. It is only half enforced: `extension-api` itself does not depend on `core`, but ten of the twelve `ext/*` implementations do, so the traits bound what an extension *provides* to the engine while the extension still reaches freely into engine internals. The seam holds in one direction.

findings.title: The TUI does not link the engine: it is a client of the app-server API
findings.description: `tui` has no dependency on `codex-core`; it drives conversations through `app-server-client` and types from `app-server-protocol`. This is the strongest layering rule the workspace enforces and it has held: the interactive frontend cannot bypass the API and must work with what a remote or embedded client would see. The one leak (direct `exec-server` and `sandboxing` imports for local helpers) is recorded under violations.

findings.title: codex-core is the god crate the repo's own guidance says not to grow
findings.description: AGENTS.md states the rule: `codex-core` has become bloated and contributors should **resist adding code to codex-core**. The manifests show the rule losing: `core` depends on 61 of 133 workspace crates, the largest fan-out in the tree, and 23 crates depend on it, so it is both the widest consumer and the second-widest provider. Extension crates that were split out (`ext/*`) mostly still link `core`, the `codex_thread`/`session` modules carry config, exec, MCP, hooks, guardian and compaction concerns, and `core` re-exports lower-layer types as its own API. The cost is that most changes rebuild and re-test the whole engine and that the compile-time seam around the engine constrains almost nothing.

evidence.snippet: Over time, the `codex-core` crate (defined in `codex-rs/core/`) has become bloated because it is the largest crate, so it is often easier to add something new to `codex-core` rather than refactor out the library code you need so your new code neither takes a dependency on, nor contributes to the size of, `codex-core`.
To that end: **resist adding code to codex-core**!

findings.recommendation: Pick the next two extractions by dependency count: hook and MCP execution (`hook_runtime`, `hook_mcp_executor`, `mcp_*`) into the existing `hooks`/`rmcp-client` crates, and the `sandboxing`/`exec` modules into the execution cluster. Make `ext/*` crates depend on `extension-api` only, so the extension seam constrains both directions.

findings.title: The vocabulary crate depends on the policy engine, the network proxy and the HTTP client
findings.description: `codex-protocol` is named and used as the shared vocabulary, and Sokrates' decomposition files it that way. Its manifest, however, pulls in `codex-execpolicy` (the rule engine), `codex-network-proxy` (the egress proxy implementation with its TLS stack) and `codex-http-client`. The uses are real: `environment.rs` embeds `RequirementsExecPolicy` and `EnvironmentNetworkPolicy`, `error.rs` wraps `HttpError`. The effect is that every one of the 68 dependents of `protocol` transitively compiles the proxy and the policy engine, and that those two crates can never depend on `protocol` types themselves, which is why `network-proxy` defines its own policy vocabulary that `core` then re-exports. The evident intent (a leaf types crate) is inverted at this seam.

findings.title: TUI skips the API layer for exec-server and sandboxing
findings.description: Against the rule that the TUI is a client of `app-server` (it does not link `core`), `tui` declares direct dependencies on `codex-exec-server`, `codex-sandboxing` and `codex-core-plugins`. These support local concerns (sandbox warnings at startup, Windows sandbox setup prompts, plugin browsing) but they mean the TUI has knowledge of the executor that a remote client cannot have, and they are the reason the exec-server has 17 dependents. Contained: three edges, all for auxiliary UI.

findings.title: No production cycles; one 21-crate cycle exists through dev-dependencies
findings.description: A manifest pass over all 133 crates finds **zero production dependency cycles**: the workspace is a DAG at build time. Adding `dev-dependencies` closes one strongly connected component of 21 crates (`core`, `exec-server`, `linux-sandbox`, `arg0`, `apply-patch`, `codex-mcp`, `core-plugins`, `tools`, `plugin`, several `ext/*`), created by `core` dev-depending on `exec-server/tests/support`, `ext/image-generation`, `ext/web-search` and `test-binary-support`, and `linux-sandbox` dev-depending on `core`. Cargo permits this and it only affects test builds, but it means the sandbox crate's tests are compiled against the whole engine.

findings.title: Engine runtime: one actor per thread, bounded submissions in, unbounded events out
findings.description: Each conversation runs as a Tokio task: `submission_loop` reads `Submission`s from a **bounded** `async_channel` and everything the session emits goes out on an **unbounded** event channel that the API layer drains. Backpressure therefore exists on the input side only; an idle or slow consumer of events lets them accumulate. Tool calls, MCP calls and sub-agents are spawned as further tasks and report back through the same event sender, which is the ordering assumption every frontend relies on.

findings.title: Three process-crossing RPC seams: app-server JSON-RPC, exec-server JSON-RPC, MCP stdio and HTTP
findings.description: Codex crosses process boundaries in three places, all JSON-RPC. **Client to engine**: `app-server` over stdio, a Unix socket, a WebSocket, or the remote-control channel. **Engine to executor**: `exec-server` over a local WebSocket or a Noise-encrypted relay, with a forwarding mode that relays frames without parsing them. **Engine to tools**: `rmcp-client` spawns MCP servers as stdio children through the executor's `ExecBackend` or talks streamable HTTP. The exec-server seam crosses the trust boundary described under security-boundaries; MCP servers cross it in the other direction (they are untrusted third-party code but run outside the command sandbox).

findings.title: Trust map: five entry points for untrusted input, one structurally enforced boundary
findings.description: Untrusted data enters Codex through five doors. **Model output** (tool calls, commands, patches) arrives in `core` from the model clients. **User project files** and `AGENTS.md` are read into context by the engine. **Third-party code** enters as MCP servers, plugins, skills and hooks through the extensibility crates. **API clients** connect to `app-server` over stdio, Unix socket, WebSocket or remote control. **Remote executors** connect to `exec-server` over a relay. Of these, only model-requested commands cross a boundary that is **enforced by structure**: they are rewritten by `codex-sandboxing` into an OS-sandboxed child process, with an `execpolicy` and `AskForApproval` gate in front. Project trust (`trust_level` per project directory) selects which approval and sandbox profile applies. MCP servers, hooks and extensions run in the engine's own trust domain as ordinary child processes or in-process code: the boundary there is policy (approval, hook trust) rather than structure. `security-scan` judges what crosses each door; this finding records where the doors are.

findings.title: Command sandbox: Seatbelt on macOS, seccomp plus Landlock or bubblewrap on Linux, restricted token on Windows, via arg0 re-exec
findings.description: `SandboxManager` picks one backend per host and rewrites the argv. On **macOS** the command is wrapped in `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec -p <profile>` with a generated Seatbelt policy (the path is pinned to defeat PATH tampering). On **Linux** the binary re-executes itself as `codex-linux-sandbox`, which launches bubblewrap with `--unshare-user --unshare-net` and read-only binds, or falls back to in-process `no_new_privs`, a seccomp network filter and Landlock filesystem rules, which the code now labels legacy. On **Windows** a restricted-token or elevated backend from `windows-sandbox-rs` is used when enabled. The single `codex` binary provides all helpers through `arg0` dispatch, and `process-hardening` disables ptrace and core dumps and strips `LD_PRELOAD`-style variables before `main`. The **executor path** (`exec-server`) refuses a request it cannot confine rather than running it open, which is the fail-closed half of the design.

findings.title: Network confinement: OS-level cut-off by default, opt-in managed egress proxy with domain policy
findings.description: Network confinement has two structural layers. The **base layer** is part of the sandbox: `network_access` is `false` by default in both `ReadOnly` and `WorkspaceWrite` policies, Linux installs a seccomp network filter or unshares the network namespace, and the child is told through `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`. The **managed layer** is `network-proxy`: an HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy with allowed and denied domain lists, `Limited` (GET/HEAD only) versus `Full` modes, optional MITM hooks, a credential broker, and a policy decider that can route decisions back to the engine (and, via `exec-server-protocol`, to a remote engine). The proxy is `enabled: false` by default and its default mode is `Full`, so it only narrows traffic when a deployment turns it on and configures domains. Sandboxed commands reach the proxy through loopback, which the Seatbelt and bwrap profiles leave open for that purpose.

evidence.note: child is told the network is off

findings.title: Escape hatches: one flag disables both gates, plus policy variants and proxy switches that widen the boundary
findings.description: Seven distinct switches relax the boundaries, all explicit. `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` sets approval to `Never` and sandbox to `DangerFullAccess` in one move (`cli` and `exec`). `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` disables the hook trust gate. `SandboxPolicy::DangerFullAccess` and `SandboxPolicy::ExternalSandbox` are protocol-level ways to run open (the latter trusts a container to confine). `network_access: true` on a policy re-enables outbound traffic. `AskForApproval::Never` removes the human from the loop. In the proxy, `dangerously_allow_non_loopback_proxy` and `dangerously_allow_all_unix_sockets` widen the managed layer. Config-requirements (`config_requirements.rs`) can pin approval policies in managed deployments, which is the gating mechanism above these flags. The naming convention (`dangerously_*`) makes the hatches greppable, which is the design's main control.

findings.title: Open defaults: Windows sandbox is disabled by default and the in-process path degrades to no sandbox
findings.description: `WindowsSandboxLevel` defaults to `Disabled`, and `get_platform_sandbox` then returns `None` on Windows. `SandboxManager::select_initial` maps that to `SandboxType::None` with `unwrap_or`, so on a default Windows install a command whose policy says `WorkspaceWrite` runs **without any OS confinement**, with only the approval gate in front. The degradation is silent at the manager level; the compensating control lives one layer up in `core::safety`, where `assess_patch_safety` only auto-approves when `get_platform_sandbox` returns a backend and otherwise asks the user or rejects, and the TUI adds a startup prompt to enable the Windows sandbox. The `exec-server` path refuses instead of degrading. So the open default is deliberate, the confined mode exists (restricted-token and elevated backends), and the single wall on a default Windows install is the approval prompt. The trade-off is documented in the enum rather than in the docs folder, whose `sandbox.md` is a link to an external page. Two smaller open defaults sit beside it: MCP servers are launched with `sandbox: None`, and the managed network proxy is off by default, so a plain configuration relies on the OS cut-off alone.

evidence.note: the compensating control: auto-approval requires a platform sandbox

findings.recommendation: Make the in-process path match the executor: when the policy requires confinement and the host cannot provide it, have `select_initial` return an error or force the `UnlessTrusted` approval policy instead of `SandboxType::None`, so the guarantee is in the sandbox layer rather than in a caller-side safety check. Headless `exec` and app-server clients get no startup prompt today. Consider a manifest-level default of `RestrictedToken` once the Windows backend is considered stable.
